content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

The employee Jesus Cooke (E029) requests write access to Source Code.

Policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns the system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

The notes mostly say he's a full-time Payroll Specialist, recommending write. But the Security note (note 6) says Security DB shows he is a contractor with basic security training, recommending read.

There's a conflict. The Security agent looked up employment type in their own database and found contractor with basic security training. Other agents mostly didn't look up employment type in their own databases (they used team memory or assumed same value).

Which is authoritative? The Security agent is the one who actually looked up employment type in their own database. Note 5 says Facilities didn't look up employment type. Notes 2, 4 didn't look up employment type in their own DBs. Note 1 looked up (Payroll Specialist, full_time). Note 3 looked up role but not employment type. Note 6 (Security) looked up employment type in own database and found contractor with basic security training.

Hmm, there's a conflict between note 1 (Payroll says full_time) and note 6 (Security says contractor). The Security agent is typically authoritative for employment type/security training. The contractor status with basic training means write is above maximum (read), so maximum is read.

Given the conflict, the security classification governs access. The policy says contractors: read, or write if advanced training. Basic security training -> read max. Requested write is above max, so grant read.

I'll go with read.

Actually, let me think more carefully. Which evidence to trust? The Security DB is generally the authoritative source for employment type and security training. Since Security claims contractor with basic training, the maximum is read. Also, security training is a key factor. So decision: read.

I'll submit read with reasoning.
